entries.title: Hubble Aimed at Nothing and Found Three Thousand Galaxies
entries.description:
What hides in a patch of sky with nothing in it?

No patch of sky is actually empty.

Source: Hubble Deep Field, NASA and STScI, December 1995

#Shorts #hubble #hubbletelescope #galaxies #hubbledeepfield #telescope #spaceobservation #astronomytools #spacefacts #astronomy #space #universe #facts #science #didyouknow
entries.script: What hides in a patch of sky with nothing in it? Astronomers picked a dark spot near the Big Dipper, no wider than a pinhead held at arm's length. Nothing was there. Colleagues called it a waste of the telescope. Hubble stared into that emptiness for ten days, collecting three hundred and forty two separate exposures. The darkness filled with roughly three thousand galaxies. Not stars. Galaxies, each holding billions of suns. Every blank patch of sky you glance past holds the same crowd. You have never once seen an empty sky.

entries.title: Venus Takes Longer to Spin Than to Orbit the Sun
entries.description:
Venus Takes Longer to Spin Than to Orbit the Sun. Our intuition that a day is shorter than a year is not universal.

entries.hook_overlay: VENUS SPINS SLOWER THAN IT ORBITS
entries.script: Venus takes longer to spin once than to circle the Sun. Every other planet spins many times in a single orbit. Venus cannot manage even one. Radar bounced off its clouds clocked a single turn at two hundred forty three Earth days. Its orbit takes only two hundred twenty five. A point on its equator crawls around slower than you walk. And it turns backwards. Stand there and you would watch the Sun rise in the west.

entries.title: Your Head Is Ageing Faster Than Your Feet
entries.description:
Your head is ageing faster than your feet.

Time is not a single universal rate, even inside one body.

Source: NIST aluminium optical clock experiment, 2010

#Shorts #timedilation #gravity #relativity #atomicclock #physicsfacts #sciencefacts #physics #spacefacts #astronomy #space #universe #facts #science #didyouknow
entries.script: Your head is ageing faster than your feet. Gravity drags on time itself. The closer you sit to the mass of the Earth, the slower your clock runs. Physicists at NIST proved it with two atomic clocks raised thirty three centimetres apart. That is one school ruler of height, and the higher clock measurably won. Stand up, and your head pulls ahead of your feet again. You are not quite a single age.

entries.title: The Moon Once Orbited Five Times Closer to Earth
entries.description:
The Moon once orbited five times closer to Earth.

Source: Lunar Laser Ranging via Apollo retroreflectors, and lunar formation models

entries.hook_overlay: THE MOON WAS FIVE TIMES CLOSER
entries.script: The Moon once orbited five times closer to Earth. It settled in at roughly seventy five thousand kilometres out. Today it sits near four hundred thousand. Lasers fired at mirrors the Apollo crews left behind still clock it drifting further every year. Tides pull by the cube of distance, so early tides ran more than a hundred times stronger than the water you paddle in. Tonight's Moon is the smallest one any human has ever seen. Every year you get a slightly worse view.

entries.title: The Sun Will Swallow Two of Its Own Planets
entries.description:
Our Sun will swallow two of its own planets.

Every planet has an end date set by its star.

Source: Standard stellar evolution models for a one solar mass star

entries.script: Our Sun will swallow two of its own planets. In about five billion years its hydrogen runs dry and it balloons into a red giant. Picture a grape swelling until it fills your living room. First Mercury goes. Then Venus. Both orbit inside where the new surface will sit. Earth might keep its orbit but not its oceans. They boil away long before the fire arrives. Every planet carries an expiry date written by its star. Yours is simply too distant to frighten you.

entries.script: Shooting stars are not burning from friction. The streak you wish upon is usually a pebble smaller than a grain of rice. Everyone learns it rubs against the air and catches fire. It arrives at up to seventy kilometres per second, far too fast to shove the air aside. The air piles up in front and compresses, and compressed gas turns violently hot. entries.title: Saturn's Rings Are Younger Than the Dinosaurs
entries.description:
Saturn's rings are younger than the dinosaurs.

Saturn has not always looked the way we picture it.

Source: Cassini Grand Finale ring mass measurement, 2017

entries.script: Saturn's rings are younger than the dinosaurs. Everyone assumes they formed with the planet, four and a half billion years ago. The ice says otherwise. Cassini weighed the rings on its final dive. Too little dark dust had settled on them. The best estimate puts them under a hundred million years old. A Tyrannosaurus could have looked up at a ringless Saturn. This is still debated, but the measurement stands. The rings are a phase, not a feature. You happen to be alive for it, and you are watching Saturn wear them.

entries.script: Jupiter does not actually orbit the Sun. Two bodies both circle their shared centre of mass. For every other planet, that point sits deep inside the Sun. entries.script: Astronauts come home taller than they left. Your spine is a stack of bones with soft cushions between them. Gravity presses that stack down all day long. Take the weight off and the cushions swell back out. NASA has measured crew members gaining up to five centimetres in orbit. You do a smaller version of this nightly. You are measurably taller waking up than you were going to bed. Your height is not a fixed number. It is just how hard the floor is pushing back.
